strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Compelling argument that object-level scene graphs are too coarse; part-level relations address genuine limitations in existing representations
Clear and expressive PAG representation: Two-level hierarchy with object and part nodes is intuitive; DAG structure naturally enforces physical realizability and assembly ordering
Substantial dataset contribution: PARSE-10K fills a real gap with 10,000 scenes, part-level segmentation, and contact graphs across 132 object categories and 17 room types
Practical and well-designed solver: Coarse-to-fine constraint satisfaction approach is sensible; clear algorithmic description with effective examples showing progressive refinement
Strong experimental results: 97.4% accuracy on visual relation MCQ (vs. 86.2% for best baseline), 86.2% on part-level contact; user study shows 47.5% preference for PAG-conditioned generation
Quality presentation: Well-organized paper with informative figures effectively illustrating PAG structure and solver mechanics
Comprehensive comparison of datasets: Table 1 clearly demonstrates PARSE-10K's unique advantages over existing resources in terms of part annotations and contact structures
weaknesses: Critically underspecified PAG construction: Real-image layout prior extraction is mentioned but barely explained; process for converting images to PAGs is essentially a black box; percentage requiring manual construction and annotation cost are vague

Limited algorithmic novelty: Solver uses standard constraint satisfaction techniques (coarse-to-fine refinement, iterative constraint accumulation); physics simulation is off-the-shelf; novelty is primarily in representation design and dataset rather than methods

Incomplete experimental evaluation: VLM comparisons are against general-purpose models rather than specialized spatial reasoning baselines; only one baseline (InstructScene) for scene generation; no ablations isolating contribution of part-level annotations

Contact model limitations not quantified: Directional-face model acknowledged to deviate on oblique contacts but no failure rate analysis provided; no alternative contact representations evaluated; impacts realism for certain object types unexplored
Missing ablation studies: No ablations on DAG structure, edge type importance, hierarchical organization, or solver stage contributions; sensitivity to constraint ordering not analyzed

Insufficient dataset analysis: Limited breakdown of diversity (17 room types mentioned but not listed); no analysis of relation type distribution; potential biases from real-image sources not discussed

Reproducibility gaps: Algorithm details sparse (constraint formulations, numerical tolerances, convergence criteria); hyperparameters deferred to supplementary; asset library construction not fully documented; 'brief dynamic simulation' duration undefined

Unquantified solver claims: 'High success rate for final validation' not quantified; assertion about pose sampling guarantees needs clarification regarding numerical precision; no computational cost or scalability analysis

Limited scope and generalization: Demonstrated only on indoor scenes; handling of articulated or deformable parts unexplored; DAG constraint may be restrictive (mutual support scenarios); generalization to other domains unclear

Small-scale user study: Only 20 participants evaluating 12 scenes each; no inter-rater reliability reported; missing quantitative generation metrics (collision rate, contact accuracy, physical stability)

strengths: Novel problem formulation addressing a genuine limitation in existing scene representations—the inability to capture fine-grained part-level interactions crucial for physical plausibility
Substantial PARSE-10K dataset contribution with 10,000 scenes, comprehensive part-level annotations, and explicit contact information, potentially enabling future research in spatial reasoning
Clear and well-designed Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) representation with intuitive hierarchical structure distinguishing object-level and part-level relations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple tasks (visual relation reasoning, contact understanding, scene graph generation) with strong baseline comparisons and user studies
Physical grounding through Sapien simulation ensures generated scenes satisfy physical constraints, providing practical utility
Well-organized presentation with detailed algorithms and extensive supplementary material supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in the Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver—implements straightforward sequential constraint satisfaction without exploring more sophisticated optimization or solver techniques
Unclear part-level contact annotation acquisition process: no specification of manual vs. automatic annotation, consistency metrics, or inter-annotator agreement, raising scalability concerns
Scene generation results are incremental rather than compelling (SGG Recall 73.2%, Precision 76.6%, F1 78.2%), with limited reporting of generation success rates or failure analysis
Absence of systematic ablation studies on PAG components, solver stages, and sensitivity to annotation quality, limiting understanding of which elements drive improvements
Part taxonomy undefined for different object categories—no explicit definition of what constitutes a 'part,' consistency metrics, or category-level analysis despite 132 categories
User study compares only against InstructScene (a 2D-to-3D baseline); missing comparisons with recent scene generation methods, limiting understanding of competitive positioning
MCQ-based evaluation tasks (Visual Relation, Part-level Contact) are artificial; strong performance may not reflect broader spatial reasoning capabilities or generalization to open-ended scenarios
Insufficient analysis of failure cases, challenging scenarios, runtime/computational complexity, and which relation types or scene configurations pose difficulties
Limited scope of scene generation baseline comparisons—only InstructScene and 3D-FRONT included, missing other recent methods for full evaluation
Modest improvements on core tasks combined with limited technical novelty raise questions about practical significance beyond dataset contribution
